impacts.caseName: The Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model are abstract under step one of the Alice framework for patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia, holding that the asserted claims of the '322 and '115 patents are directed to an abstract idea at Alice step one, requiring remand for step two analysis. The court also held that damages based on Norton's foreign sales were improperly awarded, as patent infringement damages cannot be based on extraterritorial sales.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens defendants' ability to challenge software and cybersecurity patents as abstract under § 101, and limits patent damages to domestic sales, protecting companies from inflated damages based on worldwide revenues.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in software and cybersecurity fields face heightened risk that their claims will be deemed abstract, potentially invalidating valuable patent portfolios.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting JMOL that patent claims covering humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for lack of written description and enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents covering use of humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache, reinstating a jury verdict of willful infringement by Eli Lilly. The court found the specification adequately described and enabled the claimed genus of antibodies given the state of the art.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens genus claims in the biopharmaceutical space by recognizing that well-known-in-the-art methods for creating antibodies can support broad patent claims, protecting innovators' investment in biologics development.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar competitors face greater barriers to invalidating broad antibody patent claims, potentially extending market exclusivity for branded biologics.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue third parties for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to sue for infringement—even after granting an exclusive license with shared litigation control—retains a sufficient exclusionary right to satisfy Article III standing. The court found the retained right was not rendered illusory by the license terms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Clarifies that patent owners can structure exclusive licenses while retaining enforcement rights, providing flexibility in licensing arrangements and ensuring access to courts for infringement claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face suits from licensors who retain enforcement rights even when an exclusive licensee controls commercialization, complicating standing challenges as a defense strategy.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the plaintiff presented legally sufficient evidence to establish that four asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed JMOL denial on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding there was insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known in the field. The court also reversed the patent inventorship correction, finding that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity that trade secret plaintiffs must establish with legally sufficient evidence that claimed secrets derive independent value from not being generally known, protecting defendants from overbroad trade secret assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face a higher evidentiary bar for demonstrating protectability, and companies relying on trade secret claims for competitive advantage must ensure robust documentation of the novelty of their secrets.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to selecting a processor core based on measured performance parameters are infringed when the accused process occurs entirely outside the United States, and whether a doctrine of equivalents theory was properly rejected.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed-in-part summary judgment of noninfringement of the '836 patent on extraterritoriality grounds, holding that where the accused method steps occur entirely abroad, U.S. patent law does not reach the conduct. The court reversed-in-part on the doctrine of equivalents analysis and remanded.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces territorial limits of U.S. patent law, protecting companies with global operations from patent infringement liability for processes executed entirely outside the United States.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting method claims may find it difficult to reach accused infringers who structure their processes to occur offshore, limiting enforcement options for global technology.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) had expired before Insulet filed suit for trade secret misappropriation, where the alleged misappropriation was discovered more than three years before the complaint was filed.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict and damages award in favor of Insulet, holding that the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations had expired before Insulet brought suit. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing its complaint.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clear guidance on the DTSA statute of limitations, protecting companies from stale trade secret claims and rewarding prompt enforcement of trade secret rights.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners risk losing their claims entirely if they delay filing suit, even where misappropriation is ongoing, underscoring the importance of timely investigation and litigation.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate designee may testify to facts outside personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment and that source code commands are not hearsay statements. The court found that prior sales of a device embodying all claimed limitations invalidated the patent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens defendants' ability to prove invalidity via the on-sale bar by permitting broader 30(b)(6) testimony and treating source code as non-hearsay, lowering evidentiary hurdles in patent challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges where corporate witnesses can testify about historical sales without personal knowledge, and source code evidence is more freely admissible.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for some claims while affirming eligibility for others, distinguishing between claims reciting specific technical implementations and those directed to abstract mathematical optimization. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides a nuanced framework distinguishing eligible from ineligible claims in communications technology patents, allowing well-drafted claims with specific technical implementations to survive § 101 challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies in the communications and standards-essential patent space face continued uncertainty about eligibility, with some claim formulations at risk of invalidation under Alice.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether infringement by equivalents was properly barred.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed no literal infringement, holding that the pH limitation must be measured at the standard temperature recognized in the field. The court also upheld the district court's ruling barring Actelion's doctrine of equivalents theory, affirming judgment in favor of generic manufacturer Mylan.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers benefit from a clear interpretation that scientific claim terms are measured under standard conditions, facilitating design-around efforts and ANDA filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies risk narrower claim scope when technical parameters are construed under industry-standard conditions, potentially enabling generic competition sooner.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after having missed the statutory deadline in its original action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for obtaining a mandatory stay of a district court action by voluntarily dismissing and refiling the declaratory judgment action. The ruling prevents gamesmanship in parallel ITC and district court patent proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the ruling, which prevents ITC respondents from manipulating litigation timing by refiling actions to obtain mandatory stays and delay district court proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents lose a potential tactical tool for managing parallel proceedings, increasing the burden of simultaneously litigating in both the ITC and district court.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple Watch models incorporating blood oxygen measurement functionality infringed Masimo's patents covering wearable physiological measurement devices, and whether Masimo satisfied the domestic industry requirement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watch models infringing Masimo's patents on wearable blood oxygen measurement technology, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing devices. The court found no error in the domestic industry or validity determinations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces the ITC as an effective enforcement forum for patent holders against large technology companies, validating exclusion orders that can force product redesigns or removal from the U.S. market.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies incorporating patented features into consumer products face significant import bans and market disruption through ITC enforcement actions.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy where the plaintiff was denied the opportunity to cure deficiencies in its damages case.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated summary judgment in favor of Microsoft, finding the district court abused its discretion by excluding the expert without allowing Exafer an adequate opportunity to supplement its damages theory. The case was remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from greater procedural protections ensuring they have an opportunity to cure deficiencies in damages expert reports before exclusion and summary judgment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face prolonged litigation as courts are directed to provide plaintiffs more opportunities to refine damages theories rather than granting early dispositive relief.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using access fees to fund unrelated expenses, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement for PACER fee overcharges, upholding attorneys' fees and incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives. The court rejected objections to subject matter jurisdiction, settlement fairness, and the propriety of service awards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Validates the use of incentive awards for organizational class representatives in government overcharge cases, and confirms PACER users are entitled to reimbursement for fees exceeding statutory authority.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination where a non-party to the underlying district court litigation filed IPR petitions on the statutory deadline applicable to the actual defendant, and whether the Board's claim construction was correct.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness finding for claims of the '797 patent and remanded for further proceedings, finding errors in the Board's analysis. The court also addressed the procedural question of third-party IPR filings timed to the litigation defendant's statutory deadline.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners gain additional protection against potentially coordinated IPR challenges by third parties who are not parties to the underlying litigation but time their petitions strategically.
impacts.negativeImplications: Entities using IPR as a defensive tool may face greater scrutiny when filing petitions on behalf of or in coordination with litigation defendants.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent is invalid for omission of a coinventor under 35 U.S.C. § 256 when the patent owner acknowledges the coinventor's contributions but cannot locate the coinventor to obtain consent for correction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents were invalid for failure to name a coinventor, even where the patent owner acknowledged the omission and attempted to correct inventorship but could not locate the missing coinventor. The court held that § 256(b) judicial correction requires the patent owner to meet its burden, which was not satisfied here.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can leverage inventorship defects as a potent invalidity defense, particularly where collaborative development with overseas partners creates inventorship ambiguity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies collaborating with foreign manufacturers or contractors face significant risk of patent invalidation if coinventors cannot be identified and located for inventorship correction.
